messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a 55-year-old house painter who has been married to his wife, Denise, for thirty years. On a Tuesday afternoon two years ago, he was on a ladder at a client’s home, finishing the trim on a second-story window, when his phone rang. It was his brother’s wife, and her voice was barely a whisper: “You need to come. They’re taking him by ambulance.” He jumped off the ladder, left his brushes and paint tray where they lay, and drove to the hospital. By the time he found the right floor, his brother was gone—a sudden massive heart attack, no warning, no chance to say goodbye. That drive to the hospital, the sight of the ambulance’s red lights pulling away from his brother’s house, the sterile hallway where a doctor shook his head—those images have never left him. Sometimes they come as sharp, vivid pictures: his brother’s face on a gurney, the fluorescent lights overhead, the rain starting to fall as he walked back to his truck. Other times, the emotion hits him without any image at all—a wave of grief so total it doubles him over, leaving him gasping with no clear memory attached, just the raw knowledge that his brother is gone.

Since that day, Marcus has felt the constant hum of alertness in his body. His shoulders are tight, his jaw clenched, and he startles at sudden noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming. At night, he finds it impossible to settle. He checks the locks on every door three times, walks through the house with a flashlight, and lies awake listening for the siren he dreads. Even inside his own home, the place that once felt safest, he cannot relax. He sits with his back to the wall in the living room, scanning the windows, certain that something terrible is about to happen again. His wife has asked him why he seems so jumpy, why he won’t sit beside her on the couch, and he has no words that make sense to her.

His work as a painter has become a minefield. He cannot bring himself to return to the house where he got the call—the client had to hire someone else to finish the job. Any mention of someone losing a loved one, whether on the radio, at the dinner table, or from a friend, makes his stomach drop. He excuses himself from conversations, walks out of rooms, changes the channel. Once, at a family gathering, his cousin started talking about a coworker whose father had passed away, and Marcus stood up and left without a word, driving home in silence. He has come to believe that he is no longer the same person. He used to be the one who kept the family together, the steady, easygoing man everyone relied on. Now he feels hollow, as if his brother took a part of him into the grave. He feels isolated even when surrounded by people, convinced that no one understands what it means to have your life split into before and after. A part of him is certain his life has been destroyed, that he will never feel whole again.

The consequences have accumulated. Denise has grown quiet and hurt, unsure how to reach him. Marcus has stopped taking new painting jobs that require travel or unfamiliar locations; he works only for old clients who know his situation, but even then he rushes through the job, eager to get home before dark. His income has dropped, and he has started refusing invitations to barbecues, church functions, anything where the conversation might drift toward loss or where an ambulance might pass by. He spends his evenings in the garage, organizing and reorganizing his paint cans, doing nothing really, just waiting for the next wave of grief or the next sound that will undo him.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was the night he found himself standing in the driveway at 2 a.m., fully dressed, keys in hand, ready to drive to the hospital because he thought he heard sirens. There were no sirens. Denise found him there, crying without knowing why, and she told him quietly that she was afraid for him. He is afraid too—afraid that the person he used to be is gone for good, that the images and the grief will never soften, that he will spend the rest of his life jumped up and waiting for the next loss. But somewhere underneath that fear, he holds a thin thread of hope that talking about it might loosen the grip, that he might learn to sleep through the night again, that he might one day remember his brother without being crushed by the remembering.
